strengths: Simple, practical idea: a negative cosine temperature schedule (NegCosSch) that can be folded into any temperature-dependent loss (CE or SupCon) used in OSR with zero computational overhead, making it broadly applicable.

Reasonably broad evaluation: four regular OSR benchmarks (CIFAR10, CIFAR+10, CIFAR+50, TinyImageNet) and the harder Semantic Shift Benchmarks (CUB, FGVC-Aircraft, Stanford Cars) with multiple base methods (CE, SupCon, ConOSR, ARPL), reporting AUROC, OSCR, and closed-set accuracy.

Useful analyses: UMAP visualizations of the representation space under different temperature schedules (Figure 1), an ablation over the phase parameter k in the generalized cosine schedule (Table 4), and comparison against random/step-up/Half-NegCosSch schedules, which lend some support to the design choice.

Consistent trend (Figure 4) that the benefit grows with the number of training classes, and honest limitations section acknowledging small training-class settings where the method helps less or slightly hurts closed-set accuracy.
Code availability and clear reproduction details (hyperparameters, splits, pretrained backbone choices) in the appendix.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the core mechanism is cosine temperature scheduling, already proposed by Kukleva et al. (2023) for long-tailed self-supervised learning; the contribution is essentially reversing the schedule direction and observing it works better for OSR. This is a relatively incremental scheduling tweak rather than a new method or insight.

Gains are small and inconsistent on the regular benchmarks: e.g., SupCon+NegCosSch drops AUROC on TinyImageNet (83.09 vs 83.86) and CIFAR+10/50 differences are within noise; the paper itself admits the improvement is 'insignificant' for CIFAR+50.

On the SSBs, only three prior methods (ARPL, and CE/SupCon baselines with or without LS) are compared; there is no comparison against stronger recent representation-learning-based OSR methods, so it is hard to judge competitiveness at the frontier.

Hyperparameter sensitivity: the temperature range (tau+, tau-) and period P must be selected; Section 4.1 suggests choosing ranges based on the best constant temperature found by tuning, which raises concerns about mild oracle/tuning bias favoring the proposed scheme and complicates practical adoption.

Some claims rest on qualitative evidence: the mechanistic explanation (coarse-to-fine task switching, open-set samples pushed away) is supported mainly by UMAP plots rather than quantitative measures of cluster compactness or margins.

Statistical significance is under-reported: standard deviations appear only for a subset of results (Table 3, Figure 4 error bars), while the headline Tables 1 and 2 show point estimates, and many differences are of the same magnitude as the reported std.

Baselines comparisons are partially confounded: the authors changed design choices (e.g., pretrained backbone, LS coefficients) relative to prior work, making direct comparability of improvement numbers imperfect; the ARPL rows combine several changes at once.

Writing issues: missing URL for code in footnote and Section 12, some awkward phrasing, and the framing that 'other OSR methods ... add significant computational overhead' while true for some, is overstated as a general advantage.

strengths: The proposed method is extremely simple, requires no additional parameters or computational overhead, and can be folded into existing OSR pipelines (CE, SupCon, ConOSR, ARPL) with a few lines of code; code is released.

The empirical study is reasonably broad: four regular OSR benchmarks plus the more challenging Semantic Shift Benchmarks (CUB, FGVC-Aircraft, Stanford Cars), with both AUROC, closed-set accuracy, and OSCR metrics, and comparisons with and without label smoothing.

The paper includes useful ablations beyond the main proposal: different values of k in the generalized cosine schedule, random/step-up/Half-NegCosSch schedules (Appendix Table 4), comparison against regular cosine scheduling on SSBs (Table 5), and an analysis of how gains scale with the number of training classes (Figure 4).
The qualitative analysis (UMAP visualizations in Figure 1) and the discussion of temperature effects on instance-level vs. semantic-level features are pedagogically helpful.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the core proposal is essentially the cosine temperature schedule of Kukleva et al. (2023) with the direction reversed (start low, end high). The main contribution is an empirical observation that low-to-high temperature is better for OSR, which is a fairly incremental finding rather than a new technique or insight with supporting theory.

Gains are modest and inconsistent. In Table 1, the scheme sometimes hurts (SupCon on TinyImageNet: 83.36 -> 83.09) or gives negligible improvements (CIFAR+50), and the authors themselves describe improvements on CIFAR+50 as 'insignificant'. Improvements on SSBs are typically 0.3-3.6 points with no statistical significance tests reported in the main results.

No theoretical or rigorous empirical justification for the central claim that starting with a low temperature yields a 'coarse decision boundary' that is later refined. The evidence is largely qualitative UMAP plots, which are known to be misleading for judging cluster structure and separability.

The improvement metric in Section 4.4/Figure 4 compares NegCosSch against the max over all constant-temperature baselines, which is a biased comparison that inflates apparent improvements and, as the authors admit, produces negative values in several cases.

Hyperparameter concerns: the method introduces multiple hyperparameters (tau+, tau-, P, k), and the selection strategy is ad hoc (choose tau+ = tau + Delta, tau- = tau - Delta based on regular-benchmark tuning). It is unclear whether the fixed setting (0.3, 0.1) used for SSBs would generalize, and the role of the period P is not analyzed.

Baselines are limited: only three OSR methods are tested on the regular benchmarks, and on SSBs only methods from Chen et al. (2021) and Vaze et al. (2022) are compared. Recent stronger OSR approaches are discussed but not evaluated. Additionally, the ARPL results are taken from Vaze et al. while other methods are re-implemented with a different (places365) pretrained backbone, raising comparability concerns (acknowledged in a footnote but not resolved).

Presentation issues: several typos and inconsistencies ('scheme scheme', references to Table 3 in the Appendix that do not match appendix numbering, missing URL in footnote 1 for code availability), and the abstract/intro oversell a scheduling trick as a general representation-learning contribution.

The limitation that gains diminish or reverse with few training classes (CIFAR10, CIFAR+10, CIFAR+50) substantially narrows the practical scope of the method, since many standard OSR benchmarks fall exactly in this regime.

strengths: The proposed NegCosSch scheme is extremely simple, requires no additional parameters or computational overhead, and can be folded into any temperature-modulated loss (CE, SupCon) as well as existing OSR methods (Vaze et al., ConOSR, ARPL).

Evaluation covers both regular OSR benchmarks and the harder Semantic Shift Benchmarks (CUB, FGVC-Aircraft, Stanford Cars) with Easy/Hard splits, reporting AUROC, closed-set accuracy, and OSCR — a more thorough protocol than much of the OSR literature.

Reasonable ablations: the paper compares against constant temperatures, regular cosine scheduling, random scheduling, step-up, Half-NegCosSch, and multiple values of k in the generalized cosine family, and provides UMAP visualizations motivating the scheduling direction.
The claim that improvements grow with the number of training classes is an interesting empirical observation, supported by experiments across varying training-class fractions.
Code is provided, built on established codebases, with detailed training settings in the appendix aiding reproducibility.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the method is essentially the existing cosine temperature scheduling of Kukleva et al. (2023) with the direction reversed (k=1 vs k=0 in Eq. 4). The core contribution is a one-line change whose benefit is observed empirically but not supported by theory or a principled justification for why low-to-high scheduling specifically helps open set recognition.

Improvements on the regular benchmarks are marginal and often within reported standard deviations (e.g., SupCon CIFAR10 AUROC 94.04(±0.97) vs 94.10(±0.85); TinyImageNet actually drops from 83.86 to 83.09). No statistical significance tests are reported, so many headline comparisons may be noise.

Hyperparameter selection raises fairness concerns: (τ+, τ−) ranges are chosen based on tuning on the regular benchmarks and then applied to SSBs, and per-dataset strategies differ (e.g., different (τ+, τ−) for CE vs SupCon); the risk of implicit overfitting to the benchmarks is not addressed.

Figure 4 defines 'improvement' relative to the maximum over three baselines, which biases the reported gains downward/upward in a way that complicates interpretation; the analysis of this choice is brief.

The mechanism is described qualitatively through UMAP plots; there is no quantitative analysis of representation geometry (e.g., cluster compactness, open-set distances) or theoretical grounding for why coarse-to-fine decision boundaries benefit OSR.

Gains on ConOSR and SupCon regular benchmarks are mixed (some methods improve by <0.1%), and the authors themselves concede benefits 'reduce when the number of training classes is small', narrowing the practical scope of the claim.

Missing comparisons to more recent scheduling/representation-learning OSR techniques beyond the three baselines, and the claim of generality ('can be folded into any OSR method') is validated on only three methods.

strengths: Practical and broadly applicable contribution: the proposed temperature schedules (P-NegCosSch, M-NegCosSch) can be folded into any temperature-dependent OSR loss (CE, SupCon, ARPL, ProtoCon) with essentially zero computational overhead, which is valuable for the large-benchmark (SSB) setting where extra compute/memory is prohibitive.

Careful and extensive empirical evaluation: multiple losses (CE with/without label smoothing, SupCon, ARPL, ProtoCon), multiple benchmarks (TinyImageNet, three SSBs, CIFAR benchmarks), multiple architectures (VGG32, ResNet50, Tiny ViT), 5 random seeds with reported standard deviations, and ablations over (τ+, τ−), period P, and the shift parameter k.

The mechanistic analysis (gradient of SupCon w.r.t. negative logits under temperature scaling, Section 3 and Appendix C) provides a plausible qualitative explanation for why low-to-high scheduling helps form compact clusters while keeping open-set samples distant, and the UMAP visualizations (Figure 1) support the narrative.

Honest reporting: the paper discloses failure cases (e.g., CIFAR benchmarks with few training classes, Aircraft with SupCon+LS), the discrepancy with the pretrained model of Vaze et al. (2022), and shows that even simple monotonic schedules help — giving a fairly transparent picture of where the gains come from.
Analysis of behavior with increasing number of training classes (Section 5.3) shows growing benefit on harder tasks, which strengthens the practical significance claim.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the core idea is reversing the direction of the existing cosine temperature schedule of Kukleva et al. (2023) and applying it to OSR. The paper itself shows that simple linear and exponential increases perform comparably, which weakens the claim that the 'novel negative cosine schedule' is the key ingredient; the contribution reduces largely to an empirical finding that a low-to-high temperature sweep helps.

Gains are modest and not uniformly consistent: improvements are typically 1-3% AUROC/OSCR, two cases regress relative to the constant baseline, and the CIFAR benchmarks show essentially no improvement. Statistical significance tests are not provided, so some improvements (e.g., within ~0.2-0.5% with standard deviations around that size) may not be robust.

No comparison against state-of-the-art OSR methods: the evaluation is almost entirely internal ablation of temperature schedules on fixed baselines. There is no table showing where CE+NegCosSch or ARPL+NegCosSch stands relative to recent representation-learning OSR methods (e.g., Xu et al. 2023, Bahavan et al. 2025, Li et al. 2025) on the SSBs, making it hard to assess practical significance.

The theoretical analysis is qualitative only: the gradient analysis motivates the schedule but offers no formal characterization of why low-to-high ordering is optimal, why periodicity (P-NegCosSch) sometimes helps or hurts, or how (τ+, τ−) should interact with the number of classes. The rationale for the periodic restart narrative is largely post-hoc.

Hyperparameter sensitivity is a practical concern: the method requires choosing (τ+, τ−) and P, and the proposed heuristic (τ±∆ around a tuned constant) inherits the cost of the constant-temperature hyperparameter search the method claims to complement; the schedule's superiority depends on these choices.

Reproducibility is stated but not yet delivered ('Project codes will be available'), and some experimental details (e.g., pretrained ResNet50 substituted from Zhou et al. 2017) introduce deviations from the reference protocol that complicate direct comparability with prior SSB results.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and underexplored question: how the temperature parameter in CE, SupCon, and ARPL losses affects representation learning specifically for open set recognition, extending prior work (Kukleva et al., 2023) that studied temperature schedules only in closed-set/long-tailed self-supervised settings.

The proposed method is simple, well-motivated, and has zero computational overhead; the gradient analysis in Section 3 and Appendix C provides a plausible mechanistic explanation for why low-to-high temperature schedules help push open-set representations away while compacting known classes.

Evaluation is reasonably thorough: multiple benchmarks (TinyImageNet, SSBs on CUB/Aircraft/SCars, CIFAR benchmarks), multiple loss functions (CE, SupCon, ARPL, ProtoCon), multiple architectures (VGG, ResNet50, Tiny ViT), 5 random seeds with standard deviations reported, and a broad set of schedule ablations (constant, linear, exponential, logarithmic, random, periodic/monotonic cosine variants, k-shift ablation in Eq. 5).

Honest reporting of failure cases (e.g., negligible gains on CIFAR+10/CIFAR+50, one negative case on Aircraft with SupCon+LS), and the analysis showing gains grow with more training classes adds credibility.
Clear reproducibility statement, detailed hyperparameters in the appendix, and code availability promised.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the core contribution is a temperature schedule applied to existing losses. The 'negative cosine' schedule is a trivial inversion of the existing cosine schedule from Kukleva et al. (2023), and the paper itself shows that even simple linear or exponential increases work comparably well (Table 1), which undercuts the significance of the specific proposed schedule and suggests the finding is essentially 'any low-to-high temperature warm-up helps'.

No comparison with state-of-the-art OSR methods: all tables compare only against constant-temperature versions of the same losses (CE/SupCon/ARPL with or without label smoothing). The paper cites many stronger recent OSR methods (Xu et al. 2023, Bahavan et al. 2025, Li et al. 2025, Wang et al. 2025) but never compares against them, so it is unclear whether the proposed scheme closes any gap or produces a competitive system.

Absolute gains are modest (typically ~1-3% AUROC/OSCR) and inconsistent: on several benchmarks/loss combinations the improvements are within one or two standard deviations, and Table 1 shows 'linear increase' frequently matching or beating the flagship NegCosSch, weakening the central claim that the novel schedule itself is the driver.

The evaluation protocol has a notable caveat: the pretrained ResNet50 used for the SSBs is admitted to be a different (and 'completely unrelated') checkpoint from the one used in the benchmark definition of Vaze et al. (2022), making absolute comparisons with the literature even harder and limiting external validity.

Key design choices appear tuned post hoc: the (τ+, τ−) selection strategy (Δ ≈ 0.1 or 0.2, τ+ = 2τ, τ− = τ/2) is derived from observed best performances rather than validated out of sample, raising mild overfitting-to-benchmark concerns; the ablation over P is limited (only {100, 200, 1200}).

Writing and positioning could be sharper: the paper spends substantial space on general OSR taxonomy, while the actual method occupies little space; the empirical claim that unknown samples 'are pushed away' is supported mainly by UMAP visualizations on a 10-class subset rather than quantitative representation-space metrics.

strengths: The paper addresses a practical and underexplored question: how temperature scheduling affects open set recognition (OSR), extending prior work on cosine schedules (Kukleva et al., 2023) from closed-set/self-supervised long-tail settings to open-set recognition. The finding that the direction of the schedule matters (starting low and increasing temperature outperforms the reverse) is a clear, actionable insight with a plausible mechanistic explanation (gradient analysis in Section 3/Appendix C and UMAP visualizations in Figure 1).

The proposed method is essentially free: it can be folded into any temperature-scaled loss (CE, SupCon, ARPL, ProtoCon) with a few lines of code, in contrast to mix-up, generative, or auxiliary-model OSR approaches that incur significant overhead. This makes the contribution broadly applicable and easy to adopt.

Evaluation is unusually thorough for this type of method: 4 benchmarks (TinyImageNet, three SSBs) plus CIFAR variants, 3-4 loss functions (with and without label smoothing), 5 random seeds with reported standard deviations (Tables 3-4), multiple schedule families (linear, exponential, logarithmic, random, periodic/monotonic cosine and negative cosine), ablations on (tau+, tau-), P, and k, plus an architecture check on Tiny ViT (Table 5).

The analysis in Section 5.3 showing that benefits grow with the number of training classes is valuable, as it clarifies when the method helps and explains the near-zero gains on the CIFAR benchmarks (Appendix F.6), rather than hiding unfavorable results.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the negative cosine schedule is a simple reversal of the existing cosine schedule of Kukleva et al. (2023), and even simple linear/exponential increases perform comparably (Table 1). The core contribution risks being seen as an empirical finding rather than a new technique, and the framing of 'task switching from instance-level to semantic-level' is largely a restatement of known temperature effects (Wang & Liu, 2021).

No comparison against state-of-the-art OSR methods on the SSBs or TinyImageNet. All results are schedule-vs-schedule ablations on the authors' own baselines. The paper claims the scheme 'in principle' improves other OSR methods, but never demonstrates it on top of any published SOTA OSR pipeline (e.g., the contrastive-regularization methods discussed in Section 6), so its practical significance relative to the current OSR frontier remains unclear.

The magnitude of improvement is modest and in some cases within the reported seed variance. For example, several OSCR/AUROC gains in Table 2 are 0.3-0.6 points while standard deviations in Table 4 are of similar magnitude (up to ~2 points for SupCon on Aircraft), and gains on CIFAR benchmarks are essentially zero. Statistical significance tests (e.g., paired tests over seeds) are not reported.

Some experimental setup concerns: the places365 pretrained model used for SSBs differs from the one in Vaze et al. (2022) (footnote 1), making absolute numbers not directly comparable to prior SSB literature; the batch size of 12 for SupCon on SSBs is far from standard and may confound comparisons; and Table 1 vs Table 2 baseline discrepancies (e.g., TinyImageNet constant baseline) are not clearly explained.

The qualitative analysis relies on UMAP projections of 10 selected CUB classes, which is a weak form of evidence; no quantitative metrics (e.g., inter-class/intra-class distance ratios, open-set margin distributions) corroborate the 'coarse-to-fine' narrative. Code is only promised ('will be available'), not provided.
